summary: Reports on Comcast's experiences in a July 2008 technical trial of P4P, using iTracker technology to help peer-to-peer applications work better with ISP networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: File-sharing programs pick partners to trade with, and they usually pick them at random, even when a near neighbour would be faster. This RFC reports a 2008 trial in which a cable provider told the trading software which parts of the network were close together, and the result was faster downloads and much less traffic crossing between networks.

subtitle: What Comcast's 2008 trial found when a cable provider told file-sharing software which peers were nearby.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer file sharing sends a lot of data across internet provider networks, and much of it crosses expensive links between networks.
tldr.mechanism: Comcast ran a P4P iTracker, a server that tells the peer-to-peer tracker which parts of the network are near each other, so that clients pick nearby peers first.
tldr.outcome: In the trial, downloads were 15% faster globally and 85% faster inside Comcast's own network, and incoming traffic at peering points fell by an average of 80%, with the coarsest map working best.

facts.label: Incoming traffic reduction
facts.value: An average of 80% at peering points

facts.label: Outgoing traffic reduction
facts.value: An average of 34% at peering points

today: RFC 5632 is an Informational report published in September 2009 about a trial that ran in July 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It proposes no protocol: the abstract says the technology was being considered by the IETF's Application Layer Transport Optimization working group, and the document's own next step was to share the results so that the discussion could continue.

sections.title: What the Trial Was
sections.content:
Comcast is a large broadband internet service provider in the United States that serves most of its customers over cable. In July 2008 it ran a technical trial of P4P, which stands for Proactive Network Provider Participation for P2P, with Pando Networks, Yale University and three other providers in the P4P working group of the Distributed Computing Industry Association.

The idea is that the provider tells the peer-to-peer network which parts of its own network are close together. A peer-to-peer application can then prefer a peer in the same part of the network over one on the other side of the internet. The provider expects less data to cross its own infrastructure, and the user expects a faster download. The mechanism used in the trial is called a P4P iTracker, and it was the first such trial over a cable broadband network.

The trial ran from July 2 to July 17, 2008 and used a Pando peer-to-peer client. Pando distributed a special 21-MB licensed video file, so that the effect of the iTracker could be measured. The main objective was to see what happened to peer-to-peer uploads, downloads and the provider's own network when the swarms were made more local, compared with ordinary peer-to-peer activity.

The authors also explain why they published the results. The idea had been discussed with the IETF at the Peer-to-Peer Infrastructure workshop in May 2008 and at an ALTO birds-of-a-feather meeting in July 2008, and the trial data was shared at another such meeting in November 2008. The document was written to answer the scepticism about whether P4P actually helps users and providers.
sections.plainLanguage: Comcast, a cable internet provider, tried telling file-sharing software which parts of the network sit close together, so that traders would pick a neighbour instead of someone across the internet.

sections.title: How the Trial Worked
sections.content:
A swarm is the connected set of peers exchanging pieces of a file, also called a torrent. A peer that only uploads is called a seed; one that uploads and downloads at the same time is called a leecher. The trial used five swarms. The second, third and fourth used different iTrackers, called Generic, Coarse Grained and Fine Grained. The fifth used a proprietary Pando mechanism, whose results are left out of the document because the authors wanted to focus on an open mechanism. Comcast deployed a P4P iTracker server in its production network and configured several iTracker files to give clients different degrees of locality.

The flow of information is short. A client starts a peer-to-peer session by querying a pTracker, the component that runs and manages the peer-to-peer network. The pTracker occasionally queries the P4P iTracker, which the provider maintains, and the iTracker returns network topology information. The pTracker then passes an initial list of peers to the client, so that the client can make network-aware decisions about who to trade with. Other providers either ran their own iTracker or had Pando or Yale host their iTracker files.

The clients start from the tracker-provided peers and then discover more through peer exchange. The initial peers were chosen with 90% of the guidance based on the iTracker topology and 10% random, and later peers were found by further announces or by peer exchange.

Measurement was handled by the client. Pando was enabled to capture extended logging where the client version supported it: the source and destination IP address of every transfer, the number of bytes transferred, and the start and end timestamps. That gives a precise measurement of data flow, and with it the transfer volumes and the flow rates at each point in time. Standard logging captured the start and completion time of every download and the average transfer rate the client observed. The file itself came from an origin server outside Comcast's network, which served about 10 copies; after that, all transfers, about 1 million downloads across all the providers involved, were made purely peer to peer.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks the file-sharing network's tracker for partners. The tracker sometimes asks the provider's iTracker how the network is laid out, and then suggests peers accordingly, with about nine in ten chosen from that advice.

sections.title: Three Maps of the Network Were Tried
sections.content:
Because the Comcast network is large, the authors thought a fair evaluation needed several network topologies, so that the level of effort and the design work needed to get correct statistics out of the trial could be judged. Every iTracker was configured with automation in mind, so that a successful configuration would keep updating itself rather than being maintained by hand. All of them ran on the same small server, which suggested that scaling an iTracker infrastructure would be relatively easy and inexpensive if such mechanisms were standardised and widely adopted.

The Fine Grain design was the first and the most complex. It mapped the Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) of Comcast's backbone-connected network to IP aggregates, weighted by priority and distance from one another. All peer and internet transit ASNs connected to the Comcast backbone were prioritised so that P4P traffic would prefer settlement-free and lower-cost networks before more expensive transit links, in order to lower transit costs. Each ASN and IP aggregate was then broken down further into IP subnets, down to the Optical Transport Nodes where all the Cable Modem Termination Systems reside. This gave a highly detailed description of the network to disseminate. It defined 1,182 iTracker node identifiers and produced a 107,357-line configuration file. It was the most time-consuming to build and the most complex to maintain, and the trial results indicated that this level of localisation was too high and was less effective than lower levels of localisation.

The Coarse Grain design was a limited or summarised version of the Fine Grain design. It kept the ASN to IP aggregate and weighted data for transit links, but removed all the additional localisation data, so the data sets stayed comparable without the detail of each network attached to the Comcast backbone. It defined 22 iTracker node identifiers and produced a 998-line configuration file. On cost, complexity, risk and effectiveness it was judged the optimal iTracker for Comcast. Importantly, it did not require revealing the complex internal network topology that the Fine Grain design did, and its updates were far simpler to automate, which keeps it accurate over time and keeps administrative overhead low.

The Generic Weighted design was a copy of the Coarse Grain design with one change: instead of the provider's own priorities and weights, all weights were defaulted to pre-determined parameters designed by the Yale team. Everything else was replicated from the Coarse Grain design, and gathering the information needed to support it took roughly the same level of effort.
sections.plainLanguage: Three maps were tried. The most detailed one named 1,182 places and needed a huge configuration file, and it worked worse than the simpler maps. The middle one named 22 places and was judged the best trade-off.

sections.title: What the Trial Measured
sections.content:
Raw trial data was collected by Pando and Yale and shared with Comcast and the other providers involved. Pando and Yale analysed it and delivered an analysis; Comcast analysed the raw results as well, and the raw results for Comcast were also given to Net Forecast, Inc., which performed an independent analysis.

On swarm size, downloads peaked at 24,728 per day in each swarm, or nearly 124,000 per day across all five swarms. Swarm size peaked at 11,703 peers per swarm, or nearly 57,000 peers across all five, and the number of downloads was comparable in each of the five. Table 1 of the RFC gives the cancellation rates: 3.17% for the random control swarm, 2.20% for Fine Grained, 2.22% for Generic Weighted and 1.77% for Coarse Grained. The authors note that whether the guided swarms really do achieve a lower cancellation rate is an interesting question for future research.

On download speed, Table 2 of the RFC compares the four swarms. The random control swarm averaged 144,045 bits per second globally and 254,671 bits per second inside the Comcast network. Fine Grained reached 162,344 and 402,043 bits per second, a change of plus 13% globally and plus 57% inside Comcast. Generic Weighted reached 163,205 and 463,782 bits per second, plus 13% and plus 82%. Coarse Grained reached 166,273 and 471,218 bits per second, plus 15% and plus 85%.

On network traffic, the iTracker did not appear to significantly increase uploading in the Comcast access network, since uploading was happening anyway. Uploading was 143,236 MB for the random swarm, 143,143 MB for Generic Weighted and 139,669 MB for Coarse Grained. What the iTracker did reduce was traffic crossing between networks. Outgoing traffic at peering points fell by an average of 34%, from 134,219 MB for the random swarm to 91,979 MB for Generic Weighted and 86,652 MB for Coarse Grained. Incoming traffic at peering points fell by an average of 80%, from 47,013 MB to 8,610 MB and 7,764 MB. Download activity inside the Comcast access network rose somewhat, from 56,030 MB for the random swarm to 59,765 MB and 60,781 MB, which is what one would expect when more of the trading happens close to home.
sections.plainLanguage: Files downloaded 15% faster across the internet and 85% faster inside Comcast's own network. The traffic crossing between networks fell by 80% on average, while trading inside the network rose.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC states plainly that it proposes no protocol, practice or standard. It then makes one security observation from the experiment: an internet provider can improve performance without exposing fine-grained details about the structure of its network, which might otherwise be a security concern. The Coarse Grain design, which performed best, did not reveal the internal topology that the Fine Grain design did.

On privacy, the authors argue that the iTracker makes available only network topology information. In its current form it would not let a provider work out which clients were downloading which content, or even whether the content was a song, a movie, or a title. The opt-in architecture they propose for a future standard is mentioned as a further privacy protection, so that peer-to-peer users can choose whether to take part.

Other security aspects were not considered at all, because the experiment focused on performance measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: The trial showed that a provider can give useful advice about the network without publishing a detailed map of it. The advice says nothing about what any user is downloading, but no other security question was examined.

sections.title: What the Authors Thought Should Come Next
sections.content:
The stated purpose of sharing the results was to inform the technical discussion in the IETF about how P4P iTracker mechanisms might be used. The authors note that from the user's side the mechanism can deliver faster downloads, and from the provider's side it can increase the locality of the swarms, reducing the bytes that flow over transit points while delivering an optimised experience to customers.

They also report that an internal analysis of different levels of adoption led them to believe that the value of an iTracker increases dramatically as more providers deploy one, rather than resting on a single provider. If such a mechanism were standardised, they suggest the use of provider-provided iTrackers should probably be an opt-in feature for peer-to-peer users, or at least a feature users are explicitly aware of and which is enabled by default in a particular client.

Two further directions are mentioned. A P4P iTracker combined with a peer-to-peer cache might improve download performance further, which the authors say merits further study. And the trial itself was limited: it was promising, but it points to a need for more technical investigation and trial work, exploring the effects of iTrackers with more varied client software, larger swarms, and more technically diverse content in terms of file size, file type and duration.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors think the idea works best when many providers join in, and that users should be able to choose whether to take part. They also say the trial was too small to settle the matter and calls for more work.
